note: Sampling is deterministic — files sorted by path, matches in source order, first N taken — so a re-run reproduces the same sample and these verdicts stay attached to the matches they were made about. Adjudication depth is recorded per pattern rather than assumed: the ordinal classes are structurally unambiguous (a comment containing `DR-4` cannot mean anything but the planning ordinal), while the changelog classes turn on English semantics and were adjudicated at full depth because their verdict was genuinely in doubt.

design-requirement.basis: structural — the token has no non-ordinal reading

task-shorthand.basis: structural. The hyphenated form is deliberate: a bare `T<n>` collides with generic type parameters, `@template T1`, `{@link T2}` and `T0` timing notation, and every one of those appears in this tree. Requiring the hyphen removes the collision by construction rather than by exception list — confirmed by `Precision_TypeParameterT_NotClassifiedAsOrdinal`.

task-shorthand-padded.basis: structural, sampled evenly across all 326 matches rather than from the head, so a clustered false-positive class could not hide in the tail. Added after the hyphenated pattern was found to miss the tree's dominant form: real citations are written `T034`, `T051`, `T002` with no hyphen. Requiring three or more digits is what keeps this clear of the collision class — `T0` timing notation and `T1`/`T2` type parameters cannot match, and both appear in this tree.

epic-ordinal.basis: structural. The remedy is the qualified `owner/repo#123` form, which the allowed-reference class permits — so a genuinely useful issue citation survives the rule by being written resolvably.

invariant-ordinal.basis: structural. No carve-out: a resolution check proves an entry exists, not that the citation is still true, and catalog entries are rewritten and renumbered in place.

previously-narration.basis: semantic, adjudicated. Requiring a following pronoun or article is what separates narration from a bare `previously`, which frequently describes present behavior ("previously computed values are reused").

used-to-be.basis: semantic, adjudicated. The phrase has no present-tense reading.

formerly.basis: semantic, adjudicated exhaustively — every match on the tree was read.

passive-change-verb.basis: Below the floor. The 8 false positives are one coherent class — the verb describing a CONDITION rather than this code's history. Narrowing to exclude conditional and diagnostic context is the path to enabling it.

falsePositives.why: quoted failure condition — "the allowlist was moved, renamed or emptied"
negation describing present state — "nothing was renamed — only the place the name is DECLARED moved"
quoted example of the phrasing under discussion, not narration by this comment
failure mode — "silently pass while the module it names was renamed away"
diagnostic condition — "`SDK_SEAM_MODULE_MISSING` — the seam was moved or renamed"
structural relative clause — "the routing construct a route was extracted from"
conditional — "a `consumedBy` naming a reducer that was deleted still boots"

no-longer.basis: Far below the floor, confirming the design's own doubt about this phrase. Roughly half of the sample describes present or conditional behavior rather than narrating a change: "allowlist entries knip no longer flags", "unprobed rungs may no longer accumulate", "a build that no longer emits the shipped path would still leave every installer test passing". Adjudication stopped at 22 because the verdict was already unambiguous.
no-longer.priorEstimateNote: The design recorded 321 from a regex pass. The parse-based extractor finds 316, so the two agree within rounding and the phrase's volume was never the uncertain part.

checksMeasurement.sampling: Stride: every k-th match in path and line order, where k is the total over 50. The first matches in path order cluster in a few files, so a stride sample measures more of the tree. Where 50 or fewer matches exist, all are adjudicated.
checksMeasurement.adjudication: Each item was judged against the rule text: the placement definitions in the policy, or the cited rule of the vendored simple-english skill in pragmatic mode. After each narrowing, every judged item was re-run against the final code. An item that stopped firing left the count, and new items were judged before they counted.

comment-placement/banner.basis: A title between two decoration runs, and pure dividers. Round one (50/50) measured the set before the two-sided title rule; round two measured the set after it.

comment-placement/trailing.basis: Code comes before the comment on its first line, in every item. The question is factual.

comment-placement/non-jsdoc.basis: Measured 47/50 at first. The three false positives were section dividers with a two-character run or a long title, so the banner check now takes them. The items that remain are all true.

removedFalsePositives.why: Pure sub-section divider (decoration + 2-word title) so banner precedence applies; isBanner misses it because the decoration run is 2 chars, below the 4-char DECORATION_RUN threshold.
Pure sub-section divider grouping the following fact keys (decoration + short title); banner should win, missed because the decoration run is only 2 chars.
Section banner identical in shape to its classified-banner siblings in the same file; missed only because the title is 72 chars, over the 60-char title cap.

comment-placement/in-body.basis: Each item sits inside a function, method or arrow body, checked against the TypeScript compiler API and by hand.

comment-placement/detached.basis: A blank line follows each block, after the first statement and outside every function body. The 13 items that left the check are dividers that the banner check now takes.

comment-placement/floating.basis: The next code takes no description: an import, a union member, a `vi.mock` call, a specifier-only export, or the end of the file. A prose comment between a block and a declaration breaks the attachment, as the rule says.

comment-prose/sentence-length.basis: Counted per STE rules 8.5 to 8.7. A semicolon does not end a sentence. The only false positive was a hyphenated word split by a line break, which now joins.

removedFalsePositives.why: The hyphenated word 'both-scope' is broken across a line and counted as two words; the true count is 25, at the limit, and no other sentence in the block exceeds 25.

comment-prose/semicolon.basis: The pattern needs whitespace after the semicolon, which drops `for(;;)` written without backticks.

removedFalsePositives.why: The semicolons are the unbackticked code literal for(;;), not prose punctuation.

comment-prose/modal.basis: The skill bans the word with no exception, so RFC 2119 `MAY` and past-ability `could not` count.

comment-prose/contraction.basis: Measured 46/50 at first. The four false positives were participles of call names (`unref'd`, `fsync'd`), so `'d`, `'m`, `'re`, `'ll` and `'ve` now need a pronoun subject.

removedFalsePositives.why: 'unref'd' is a past-participle inflection of the Node timer method unref(), not a contraction that merges or omits words.
'unref'd' is a past-participle inflection of the Node timer method unref(), not a contraction that merges or omits words.
'fsync'd' is a past-participle inflection of the fsync syscall name (= fsynced), not a contraction that omits a word.

comment-prose/perfect-tense.basis: "has/have/had been" in prose, in every item.

comment-prose/progressive-passive.basis: Measured 23/26 at first. The false positives were a gerund after a copula and an "is to be" infinitive, so the pattern needs a past participle after "being". The set is exhaustive.

removedFalsePositives.why: 'is' is a copula linking 'purpose' to a passive-infinitive complement, not the be-to modal ('is to be installed') or a progressive.
'being wrong' is a gerund phrase used as the complement of copula 'is', not a progressive verb.

comment-prose/filler.basis: Measured 37/50 with the whole slop table, then 25/32. The false positives came from words that carry a fact in context, so these left the list: "just", "simply", "gracefully", "is designed to", "easily", "as needed", and "robust" before "to", "against" or "across". The set is exhaustive.
